ranked.name: 1. Closed loop present but no resolvable hole: a yielded or incomplete spring (partial duplex closed by invisible ssDNA, or one apex kink folding the arc into a narrow V). This merges expert-1 H2, expert-2 H3 and expert-3 H3.
ranked.why: This is the only hypothesis that fits both the gel as the user reports it and the EM without special pleading. It takes the gel at face value: the ~30 kDa band needs cDNA, and if the 1-Tet control was matched it also needs the second Tet, so the band is the ss loop carrying cDNA. In EM it produces no hole. The duplex is short or straight and returns to sfGFP through ~10-20 nt of ssDNA, which is invisible at 200 kV in this ice. Alternatively, a single kink relieves almost all of the ~23 kBT arc energy, because the arc ends hang on flexible TEG hinges rather than closing on themselves, unlike a minicircle. The result projects as a dot plus an ~80-115 Å rod with a gap below the 12 Å resolution limit. It also fits the ~half of conjugates that stay at ~26 kDa despite equimolar cDNA, if threading or strain stalled them. Weaknesses: the specific EM support is soft. 'Dot + long rod ~100 Å' is clipped by the 200 Å window. Several anchor 'dot + short rod' classes (e.g. 19, 25, 11) show a rod segment offset from the dot or not aimed at it, which looks like a neighbouring rod cut off by the 273 Å box rather than a stub. The 1-Tet control was not run on this gel.

ranked.name: 2. Few or no loops in the grid sample: dot-at-rod-end particles are linear sfGFP–dsDNA mono-adducts (plus free duplex). Causes: cDNA hybridised before the second click (J of a stiff 50 bp duplex is ~1e-13 M), a dead or reduced second Tet, or a slow BCN click. Merges expert-1 H3, expert-3 H1 and part of expert-2 H4.
ranked.why: This fits all of the EM: no rings, abundant full-length free rods with the B-DNA repeat (143 Å, matching the W3 control), dot-at-end classes, and dot pairs at chance level. The kinetics strongly favour it if the three components were co-mixed: hybridisation takes under a second at 10 µM, the first Tet-BCN click takes minutes to hours, and closing a pre-formed duplex is essentially impossible. Its main cost is that the user's 1-Tet control has to be non-equivalent (different gel, lower conjugation yield, mostly (1-Tet)2 dumbbells, or a different order of addition). A second problem: the dot-centred anchor stream, which is unbiased for rods, is dominated by dot pairs and single dots (80%) and shows almost no dot + full-length-rod classes. That is awkward if ~30-40% of sfGFP carried a 167 Å duplex, though window clipping and rotational blur of weak rods may hide them.

ranked.name: 3. ss loops close efficiently but cannot be fully hybridised (threading or strain block, partial hybrids stripped in SDS). The ~30 kDa band is open mono-adducts that did hybridise, and the persisting ~26 kDa band is ss loops. Merges expert-2 H2, expert-3 H4 and expert-2 H4.
ranked.why: This explains why ~44% of lane-3 signal stays at ~26 kDa even though cDNA is at least equimolar. It also explains why most anchor-stream dots carry no visible rod (an ss loop is invisible) and why no rings appear. It conflicts with the reported 1-Tet result as directly as hypothesis 2 does, and Zocchi-type springs show that a linear complement can be hybridised onto a protein-closed ss loop of this size, so a total block is unlikely. The TCO-PEG5k chase separates it cleanly from hypothesis 1.

ranked.name: 4. Rings exist in solution (the gel's ~20-28% of sfGFP) but open, melt or deform on the grid: air-water interface (AWI) adsorption and surface forces, sfGFP strand 133-149 unravelling under the 25-36 pN load, or dilution and low salt in the grid buffer. Merges expert-1 H4, expert-2 H1 and expert-3 H2.
ranked.why: The density of ~4,500 dots/µm², ~20-25x bulk, shows that the imaged population is adsorbed at the AWI. The strained arc is the species most likely to fail there, and unstrained free rods survive, which fits. But nothing in the data points specifically to destruction. Dots near rods are only modestly lower in LoG contrast, and the dot classes are compact. On the grid its EM signature is the same as hypothesis 1, so only a solution-state readout or a change of support can test it.

ranked.name: 5. Intact rings are on the grid but seen near edge-on, for example because AWI-pinned sfGFP holds the charged DNA arc upright into the bulk, and are filed as 'dot pair + faint thread' or dot–rod–dot classes (rod 186, 199, 101; anchor 5, 101).
ranked.why: Edge-on, a 106 Å ring projects as a ≤110 Å bar. The far rim, where the arc runs along the beam, adds up to a second faint 'dot', which is the dot_pair_thread look (16% of rod picks; the 57k class 186). This is the only way intact full rings survive the no-hole result. It requires a strongly preferred orientation, and the dot spacing in these classes (~70-100 Å) overlaps the chance nearest-neighbour distance (~75 Å) in this crowded ice.

ranked.name: 6. Intermolecular sfGFP–DNA–sfGFP dumbbells and short chains carry a large share of the 2-Tet-specific conjugate; a dot-centred 200 Å window turns them into 'dot + rod'.
ranked.why: This is a real co-product: there are high-MW bands in lanes 2-3, both partners are bifunctional, and it is favoured if the duplex forms before the second click. But it predicts bands at ≥45 kDa, not the ~30 kDa band. The far-end density bump in class 78 is a weak hint of it. Treat it as a modifier of hypothesis 2, not the main explanation.

ranked.name: 7. The ~30 kDa signal is mostly a gel artefact or sfGFP conformer (lane 1 already has a faint band at the same row; saturated 8-bit image).
ranked.why: This can only modify the size of the cDNA-dependent rise (net ~20-28 points rather than 40%). It cannot produce the rise on its own.

ranked.name: 8. Intact rings in face-on or tilted views are present but both pickers and 2D missed them.
ranked.why: Simulated L6_loop50 rings in this ice and CTF are obvious. DNA contrast is high (the 34 Å repeat is visible). A ring 106 Å across fits inside both windows, and the anchor stream centres on the dots that rings would carry. At the gel's abundance (~0.5-0.7 M particles), even 1% recovery would have produced a ring class.

em_analyses: A1 (top discriminator, 1 vs 2/3): window-free length of attached DNA. Particles: rod-stream dot-at-end classes (e.g. 31, 48, 61, 4, 36, 128, 82, 78) and anchor dot+rod classes (5, 19, 25, 11, 101, 135). References: rod_no_dot classes and the W3 free-duplex-control particles. Re-extract at a ~448 Å box recentred on the rod midpoint (dot centre + L/2 along the 2D axis) and run 2D with a ≥360 Å inner window. In parallel, trace each rod on denoised micrographs with no classification. Measure the half-max rod-body length excluding the dot, the number of 34 Å repeats, any bowing, and the dot-to-rod-end gap and angle. Attached length equal to free/W3 rods (median ~140-150 Å, 4-5 repeats, KS not different) with a broad hinge angle means linear adducts (2 or 3), and full-duplex loops are not on the grid. A distinct mode at ~35-115 Å with ≤3 repeats and a fixed exit angle means incomplete or kinked loops (1, or 4 after damage).

A2: width and integrated-density profile along the attached rod, outward from the dot, compared with free rods at matched defocus. Width ≥40 Å and ~2x density per Å near the dot, tapering to 1x at the tip, with the 34 Å repeat lost, means a kinked V (1). A uniform 1x profile means a single duplex (1 with an ss return, or 2/3).

A3: selection-free census of dots carrying a rod end. Start from the unbiased dot detector (~330 per micrograph) and rod traces made before any 2D. For each dot, score a rod end within 15-35 Å, against shift and rotation nulls matched in distance from the rod and in local density. Report the excess fraction of dots with an attached rod and the length distribution of those rods. Hypothesis 2 predicts ~25-40% of dots (the 30 kDa band) carrying full ~145 Å rods. Hypothesis 3 predicts the excess equals the 30 kDa fraction, with full-length rods and most other dots bare. Hypothesis 1 predicts the excess sits on short rods. No excess means the conjugate DNA is mostly ss or invisible (1, 3 or 4).

A4: run the W3 free-DNA control through the identical rod picker, the 200 Å-window 2D and the script-17 end-blob count, with one end rule in every stratum (fit the body profile, not half-max). DNA-only rods showing the ~27% one-ended blob means the rod_no_dot blob is a DNA, BCN or processing artefact. Absence of the blob means those 'free' rods are really mono-adducts, which raises hypothesis 2.

A5 (edge-on ring test for 5): take dot_pair_thread and dot–rod–dot particles (rod classes 186, 199, 101; anchor 5, 101). Compare the pair-separation histogram with the dot-detector g(r) under a shift null, and measure thread density per Å against a single duplex. Edge-on rings predict a narrow excess at 85-110 Å, a thread at ≥2x duplex density with no 34 Å repeat, and a brightened far rim. Run heterogeneous refinement with ring, dumbbell and decoy references. Chance pairs give a smooth g(r) and a noise-level thread.

A6 (cap on hypotheses 8 and 4): template-pick all micrographs with L6_loop50 projections at 0/30/50/70/90° tilt, plus a straight-rod decoy template, and run 2D with a 300 Å window, including particles from the junk, ice and unassigned classes. Report an upper bound on the ring fraction per micrograph relative to dots. Any ring class present in the ring picks and absent from the decoy picks revives hypotheses 4/5/8 in part.

A7 (AWI, hypothesis 4): stratify micrographs into tertiles by ice thickness (CTF-fit or energy-filter-free intensity proxy). Compare dot-with-rod fraction, attached length (A1) and any curved or ring classes between tertiles. Rings or longer attached duplexes enriched in thick ice support hypothesis 4.

A8 (dumbbells, hypothesis 6): from window-free traces, count rods with a dot within 35 Å of both ends (dot separation ~190-220 Å, collinear), against a null. Include the excluded dot_pair_thread (83,949) and dot_pair (37,380) particles.
bench_tests: B1 (cheapest, needed first): one gel, same day, non-saturating exposure. Lanes: 1-Tet and 2-Tet x {no DNA, 2-BCN ssDNA, ssDNA then cDNA after the click is complete, all three premixed}, plus 2-Tet + mono-BCN ssDNA + cDNA as a linear reference if available. Image GFP, then post-stain with SYBR Gold, or use Cy5-cDNA, to see which bands carry cDNA. Outcomes: a ~30 kDa band only for 2-Tet at matched 1-Tet conjugation yield means it is loop-specific (supports 1/4). A 1-Tet shift means it is not (supports 2/3). A band that forms only with ssDNA-first means the premixed sample has no loops, so record which order the grid sample used.

B2: TCO-PEG5k chase (already in the reagent table) after the click and before cDNA. Open adducts with a free Tet gain ~+5 kDa (large SDS shift); closed loops do not. Optionally also chase with a methyltetrazine dye to label any dangling BCN. Then add cDNA to the chased sample. The 30 kDa band forming from the un-PEGylated (closed) population supports 1/4. Forming from the PEGylated (open) population supports 3. Few closed loops overall supports 2.

B3: S1 or mung-bean nuclease on the lane-3 mixture and on the linear reference, then run the fluorescent gel plus SYBR. If the ~30 kDa species loses DNA (moves toward 26 kDa or free sfGFP, or releases defined fragments), it has ss gaps, i.e. a partial or yielded loop (1). If it is resistant like the linear duplex, it is fully paired (a full ring, or 2). Weak cleavage at one site suggests a kink.

B4: thermal or strain readout of the ring. Measure the SYBR or FRET melt of the ~30 kDa species against the linear reference. A full strained ring should show a Tm depression of several °C. A split complement (two 25-mers, no threading needed) or a cDNA with a deliberate 10-15 nt gap serves as the positive control for a yielded, V-type loop.

B5 (only if B1-B3 say full rings exist in solution): image the gel- or SEC-purified ~30 kDa species at 0.5-1 µM on graphene-oxide cryo grids (or with fluorinated octyl maltoside), using a small screening collection. Separately, collect a few hundred 30-40°-tilted movies on a remaining grid from the original batch. Rings appearing on the support but not on open holes support 4. Rings appearing only on tilted micrographs support 5.
B6 (optional): a concentration series (0.5, 2 and 10 µM at 1:1:1). Intramolecular loop yield stays constant across concentration, while dumbbells and chains (6) scale with it.
ruled_out: Intact open rings (face-on or tilted up to ~50-70°) on the grid at anything near the gel-implied abundance. The gel implies ~20-28% of sfGFP, i.e. ~65-90 per micrograph and ~0.5-0.7 M particles. Zero hole-bearing classes in 304, simulated rings that are obvious in this real ice, and a ring diameter (~106 Å) that fits inside both 2D windows cap visible rings at roughly ≤1-5% of sfGFP.
'The picker or 2D missed every view' as an explanation of the null result. It is not credible for face-on or tilted rings; only a strong edge-on preferred orientation (hypothesis 5) remains.
A gel or conformer artefact as the sole cause of the cDNA-dependent ~30 kDa band. The rise is ~20-28 net points and depends on cDNA. Lane 1's faint band at the same row only lowers the net size.

Using 'dot + long rod ≈ 100 Å DNA' as evidence of a shortened duplex. Those far ends sit 64-99 Å from the alignment centre inside a 100 Å-radius window, so the length is clipped. The anchor 'dot + short rod' classes are not clean stub evidence either: several show a rod offset from the dot or not aimed at it, consistent with a neighbouring rod cut by the 273 Å box.

Reading the co-localisation statistics as evidence for or against covalent end attachment. rod_no_dot is not a dot-free control (one-ended blob in 27% of its particles), the nulls are biased, and the verdict is NOT SHOWN either way.

The 1-Tet negative, by itself, as proof of full 50 bp rings. Even if valid, it shows only that the band needs a protein-closed loop. It cannot separate a full ring from a partially hybridised or kinked loop.
Any test of the MD Euler-buckling vs Zocchi-yielding question from the current EM. No ring has been observed, so the data are silent on how the spring yields.
judge.summary:
Your gel shift is real. The ~30 kDa band appears only with cDNA. If the 1-Tet control was run at matched conjugation yield, the band also needs both tetrazines, which points to a DNA loop closed through the protein. But the gel cannot tell whether that loop holds a complete 50 bp duplex or only part of one.

The cryo-EM firmly rules out one thing. Intact open rings at the gel's abundance (about 20-28% of sfGFP, roughly 70 per micrograph) are not on the grid. Simulated rings are obvious in your ice, and none of the 304 classes shows a hole.

Three explanations remain:
1. Loops formed, but the duplex is incomplete or kinked, so each looks like a dot with a short rod.
2. Few loops formed in the grid sample, for example because cDNA paired before the second click, so you see ordinary linear dot-on-rod conjugates.
3. Rings opened at the air-water interface.

Cheapest next steps, all on one gel:
- 1-Tet vs 2-Tet, with and without cDNA, adding cDNA after the click vs premixed.
- A TCO-PEG5k chase to count closed loops.
- S1 nuclease to test whether the loop is fully paired.

Please also note which mixing order the grid sample used. On the existing EM data, re-measure attached DNA lengths with a larger, rod-centred window and compare them with the free-DNA control.

hypotheses.name: H1. Closed, fully hybridised ring (smoothly bent or kinked) is present at roughly the gel's abundance, and the EM pipeline misses it
hypotheses.mechanism: Geometry is self-consistent: 50 bp = 167 Å contour. An 80 Å end-to-end span (Cβ–Cβ 31 Å plus TEG–BCN–Tet linkers) forces a 223° arc with R = 43 Å. Bending energy is B·L/2R² = 22.6 kBT (Lp 50 nm), and the bending torque is B/R ≈ 47 pN·nm. That torque is above Zocchi's critical torque for a kink (31–36 pN·nm continuous, 27 nicked). The energy is like a ~130 bp minicircle, but the local curvature is like an ~81 bp minicircle, which is the regime where kinks appear in 64–94 bp minicircles (Du 2008; Demurtas 2009 cryo-EM). Hybridisation (~50 bp × −2.5 kBT, about −120 kBT) easily pays for 23 kBT, so the ring can close. My estimate is that 10–60% of rings carry a kink or bubble at the apex. MD at 100 ns is far too short to rule out kink nucleation. Projection: a smooth ring has outer diameter ~106 Å and a hole ~66 Å with sfGFP in the gap. A kinked ring is a teardrop or triangle (two ~83 Å arms opening at ~57°) that still encloses a ~40–60 Å hole. Kinking does NOT turn the ring into a straight rod plus dot.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Directly. A ring-specific 1:1:1 species needs both Tets, so 1-Tet gives no shift, and its rigid closed duplex slows it to ~30 kDa. Net new fluorescence is ~20% at 30 kDa above the lane-1 baseline.
hypotheses.explains_em: Poorly. If ~20% of sfGFP were rings, there would be ~65 per micrograph and ~0.5 M in the dataset. AWI adsorption (dots ~25× the bulk density for 10 µM in 30 nm ice) favours face-on, flat views, which show the hole best. The only escape is that rings are seen near edge-on, where they project as a ≤110 Å rod with the protein blob inside one end or at the centre. That would fit the rod_no_dot 'blob 18–31 Å inside the + end' (27% of particles) and the class-160 central blob. Tilted views with holes (>50% of random orientations) would also have to be lost to the junk or ice classes.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) Edge-on ring classes must be ≤ ~110 Å long. Any rod_no_dot or dot class of 120–146 Å cannot be a ring. (2) Edge-on rings superpose two arcs with different helical phases, so the 34 Å repeat is absent and width grows with tilt (20 + 86·sin t Å). The 28–34 Å widths should anticorrelate with repeat visibility. (3) Re-classify the junk (12%) and ice-adjacent particles with a 250–300 Å window, plus a ring-template pick, and look for elliptical holes. A ring class of ≥1–2% of particles would have been found among the 304 classes, so the current null already caps full rings at roughly ≤5% of sfGFP.
hypotheses.bench_test: Use intact ESI-MS on the conjugate (the lab has already resolved 141/281 Da). A bis-adduct (intramolecular, 2 N2 lost) is 28 Da lighter than a mono-adduct with a free BCN. This tells ring from lariat directly. Then put a 4–5 nt ss gap (nick/gap) in the cDNA to relieve the strain, and check whether rings appear in EM and whether the 30 kDa band persists.

hypotheses.name: H2. Ring closes, but the duplex is incomplete (topological threading trap plus strain-driven fraying): a short straight or gently curved duplex tethered back to sfGFP by invisible ssDNA
hypotheses.mechanism: If the ssDNA clicks to both Tets first (a 50-nt ss loop forms fast, effective molarity ~mM), the loop is a closed circle through the protein. A linear cDNA can then wind its 4.8 helical turns only by threading its free end through the shrinking protein–DNA hole once per turn. This is the known strain and threading penalty for complements of small circles (Kool's circular oligos). Duplexes form readily up to 1–3 turns, and the final threading steps are slow. At equilibrium, the marginal bending cost of the last bp is ~1–2 kBT/bp. That is close to the ~2.5 kBT/bp hybridisation gain at 150 mM Na+/Mg2+, and above it at low salt or for AT-rich ends. So at least 4–10 bp of fraying at the apex or ends is expected in low-ionic-strength EM buffer. A state with ~40 bp plus 10 nt ss costs ~25–30 kBT, against 22.6 kBT for the full ring, so the two are within a few kBT. A state with 30 bp straight plus 20 nt ss costs ~50 kBT and exists only as a kinetic trap. Projection: about 36–42 bp (120–140 Å) of near-straight or slightly bowed duplex with sfGFP at one end. The far end returns to the protein through 8–14 nt of ssDNA that is invisible at 200 kV in thick crowded ice. This reads as 'dot at end of a rod' with no hole.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Yes. The species needs both Tets (1-Tet negative) and carries cDNA, so it shifts. Partial threading also explains why only ~40% of conjugate shifts while ~60% stays at 26 kDa (ss loops or lariats not yet hybridised). If the cDNA is threaded at least once, it is mechanically locked and cannot fall off during SDS-PAGE, which may be why a linear 1-Tet duplex behaves differently.
hypotheses.explains_em: Yes. There are no holes, and dot-at-end-of-rod is the commonest DNA class (26%). Rods attached to dots are shorter than free rods. The one-ended blob inside rod_no_dot ends fits sfGFP held against the duplex end by a short linker.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: Re-extract dot+rod particles centred on the rod midpoint with a ≥320 Å inner window. The DNA length distribution should then peak at 30–42 bp (100–140 Å) and sit below the free-rod (W3 duplex control) distribution even after matching foreshortening. Helical-repeat counting should give 3–4 turns rather than ~5. Rods should show slight consistent bowing toward the dot side. The far end should lie within ss reach of the dot (≤ ~100 Å). On micrographs, a faint ss density or 'thread' from the far end back to the dot should appear in a subset (compare the dot_pair_thread classes, 16%).
hypotheses.bench_test: Run two orders of addition: click ssDNA first, then add cDNA, versus the reverse. Use Cy5-cDNA and a FAM/BHQ hairpin-free FRET pair placed at the duplex ends to measure the hybridised fraction and the Tm depression of the strained loop against the linear 1-Tet conjugate. Use S1 or mung-bean nuclease to probe the ss gaps and kink sites: cleavage of a ring conjugate leaves sfGFP-bound fragments of defined length on a denaturing gel.

hypotheses.name: H3. Little or no ring: EM dot+rod particles are linear mono-adducts and free duplex, and the ~100 Å vs ~143 Å length gap is a 2D-window and foreshortening artefact
hypotheses.mechanism: If cDNA was present during the click (1:1:1 co-mix), hybridisation takes seconds (k_on ~1e6 M⁻¹s⁻¹ × 10 µM), while the first Tet–BCN click takes minutes to hours. The DNA is therefore a rigid 50 bp duplex before the second click. The effective molarity of the second, intramolecular BCN is about 0.8 mM × e^-23 ≈ 1e-13 M, so ring closure is negligible against 10 µM intermolecular partners and mono-adducts dominate. The EM length gap does not discriminate. In dot classes the alignment centre sits on the dot, and the 200 Å inner window soft-masks density beyond 100 Å. A 167 Å duplex therefore shows only ~85–100 Å past the dot edge (the review measured far ends at 64–99 Å from the box centre). Random tilt alone gives a mean projected length of π/4·167 ≈ 131 Å. 'Dot + short rod' at 87 Å total is foreshortened or clipped duplex.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Only if the 1-Tet negative is not what it seems. Lane 1 already has 20% at ~30 kDa (a non-native or alternative sfGFP species), so the 'new' band partly co-migrates with a protein-only band. A linear mono-adduct plus cDNA should shift for 1-Tet as well, unless the 1-Tet conjugation yield was lower, the shift was hidden in the baseline band, or the order of addition differed between experiments. This hypothesis needs the 1-Tet control to be weaker than reported.
hypotheses.explains_em: Fully. No rings, abundant free rods (19%) with the B-DNA repeat, dot at one end (26%), a one-ended blob, no excess dots at far ends, and chance-level dot pairs (mean nearest-neighbour distance at 4,500/µm² is ~75 Å).
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: After re-centring dot+rod particles on the rod midpoint with a ≥320 Å window, rod length should match the free-rod and W3 duplex-control distribution (~140–150 Å projected, 5 helical turns), with no bowing. The dot should sit ~20–40 Å beyond the end on a flexible TEG–BCN–Tet tether, with an angular spread about the rod axis. Far ends should carry no dot above a window-matched null.
hypotheses.bench_test: Run on one gel, side by side, at matched conjugation yield: 1-Tet versus 2-Tet, each ± cDNA, with ssDNA-first versus pre-hybridised addition. Post-stain with SYBR Gold, or use Cy5-cDNA, to see where the duplex actually runs. Add intact MS for the 28 Da bis- versus mono-adduct difference. If the 30 kDa band appears only when ssDNA is clicked first, H3 is falsified for the gel but not for the EM grid if the grid used the co-mixed sample.

hypotheses.name: H4. Rings exist in solution but are destroyed, deformed or excluded at the air–water interface during grid preparation
hypotheses.mechanism: About 4,500 dots/µm² against ~180/µm² expected for 10 µM in 30 nm ice means the imaged population is AWI-adsorbed (Noble 2018; D'Imprima 2019). A strained ring stores ~23 kBT and pushes on the 133/149 Cβ pair with 25–36 pN (MD, unyielded) or a few pN (yielded). Interfacial forces (surface tension × nm ≈ tens of pN) plus partial sfGFP unfolding at the AWI can relieve the strain. This could happen by local unfolding of the 133–149 strand region (GFP helix detachment occurs at ~35 pN; Dietz & Rief 2004) or by melting the strained duplex on a hydrophobic interface. Either way, rings become open 'dot + rod' or 'dot + ss + short duplex' objects. Rings may also adsorb less than free duplex, so the grid under-samples them.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Yes. The gel reports the bulk solution, where rings may be ~20% of sfGFP.
hypotheses.explains_em: Yes, but only by fiat. No rings, many dot+rod objects, fuzzy or low-contrast dots near rods (LoG z 5.1–5.5 against 6.1–6.9 for isolated dots, from the review).
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: Composition should vary with local ice thickness (CTF-derived or per-micrograph): thick-ice micrographs should be enriched in non-AWI particles and show more dot-at-end or closed objects. Dots attached to rods should have lower contrast or less compact 2D averages than free dots (partially unfolded barrel). Rod curvature should be absent across all classes (flattened duplexes).
hypotheses.bench_test: Prepare grids on graphene oxide or with a surfactant (for example 0.05% fluorinated octyl maltoside), and blot faster (chameleon-style), then compare ring counts. In parallel, use a bulk-solution readout that never touches an AWI: native gel or SEC of the reaction, and liquid AFM on mica, to find the ring fraction before vitrification. Re-run the fluorescent gel on an aliquot taken through the grid buffer exchange and dilution, to show that the 30 kDa species survives the EM buffer.

hypotheses.name: H5. Intermolecular products (sfGFP–dsDNA–sfGFP dumbbells and short chains) carry much of the 2-Tet-specific conjugate, and the 2D window splits them into 'dot at one end of a rod'
hypotheses.mechanism: Once the DNA is duplexed, the second BCN end cannot reach its own protein (J ~1e-13 M). It reacts with a second 2-Tet sfGFP at 10 µM, and each 2-Tet protein can link two duplexes, giving dumbbells and oligomers. A dumbbell has dots ~190–210 Å apart, joined by a straight 50 bp rod. With the alignment centre on one dot and a 100 Å window radius, the second dot falls outside the window, so 2D shows 'dot + rod' with the far end clipped.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Partly. Dumbbells and chains need both Tets (1-Tet cannot chain) and form only when there is DNA. They predict cDNA-dependent bands at ≥45–60 kDa, matching the faint high bands in lanes 2–3, not the 30 kDa band. So H5 is a co-product alongside H2 or H3, not a full explanation.
hypotheses.explains_em: Dot at end of a rod, a capped DNA length (~100 Å), and no rings. Far-end tests were run inside the window, so they could not see a far-end dot at ~200 Å.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: On micrographs, using rod coordinates, count dot pairs collinear with a rod at 180–220 Å separation (one dot at each end) against a shift or rotation null matched to box-centre distance. Expect an excess if dumbbells exist. Re-classify with a 400 Å box and a 360 Å window: dumbbell classes should appear, including within the dot_pair_thread (83,949) and dot_pair (37,380) classes that were excluded from the rod set.
hypotheses.bench_test: Run a concentration series (0.5, 2, 10 µM at fixed 1:1:1). Intramolecular ring yield is concentration-independent, while dumbbells and chains scale with concentration. Read out on the fluorescent gel plus SYBR Gold, and by SEC-MALS.

hypotheses.name: H1: Closed, fully hybridised springs are the ~30 kDa band; they exist in solution but are destroyed or missed on the grid
hypotheses.mechanism: Reading of the gel (the user's): ssDNA clicks to both Tets, and the ss loop runs at ~26 kDa. cDNA fully hybridises about half of the loops into the strained 50 bp ring, which runs at ~30 kDa. The ring may be retarded by topology: small closed DNA rings run slow in polyacrylamide, as minicircles do, because gel fibres can thread through the hole. Open species are assumed to run at ~35 kDa, or to co-migrate whether hybridised or not. This would fit the 1-Tet result. On the grid the ring is lost or unrecognised. Possible causes: adsorption at the air-water interface plus 25-36 pN of stored strain, giving fraying, unzipping or peeling of strand 7 of sfGFP (site 149 is next to His148); picker templates (rods and dots) that do not pick rings; or rings filed into the junk/ice classes.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Explains everything if the 1-Tet control is valid. The new band depends on cDNA and on the second Tet. Lane-3 densitometry: ~31% of fluorescence at ~30 kDa against ~3% in lane 2. So ~25-30% of folded sfGFP would be closed hybridised springs, and ~half of the ~26 kDa loops converted.
hypotheses.explains_em: Poorly. At ~330 sfGFP per micrograph, the gel's ~25-30% would mean ~80-100 springs per micrograph (~700k over 8,036 micrographs). In the label guide's simulations, face-on and 50°-tilted rings have an obvious hole, and that hole shows in most random orientations. Zero enclosed-hole classes in 304 therefore needs near-complete loss on the grid or near-complete picking failure. Edge-on rings project as a ~90-110 Å rod with the dot at one end, so a small part of 'dot + rod' could be rings, but only with strong edge-on preferred orientation, which is unlikely for a flat ring at the air-water interface.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) Template-pick with the projected L6_loop50 ring at several tilts (in the label guide). Run 2D on particles from the junk, ice and unassigned classes of both streams with a 250-300 Å window. Rings should appear at roughly 10^4-10^5 particles. (2) In the dot-anchored stream, dot + short rod classes (87 Å) should show faint arc density curving back toward the dot when re-classified with a larger window and finer classes. (3) A count of hole-like closed contours on denoised micrographs should exceed the crowding null by ~tens per micrograph.
hypotheses.bench_test: Purify the ~30 kDa species (anion exchange, or cut and elute the band in native conditions) and image it by negative stain and liquid AFM, where an ~11 nm ring with a hole is easy to see. Re-make cryo grids from the purified fraction, both on graphene oxide and with 0.05% fluorinated octyl maltoside, to reduce air-water-interface damage. Separately: does the ~30 kDa band survive 5 min at 37/50/65 °C in SDS buffer before loading? A strained ring melts at a lower temperature than the open hybrid.

hypotheses.name: H2: The ~30 kDa band is the open hybridised mono-adduct; the leftover ~26 kDa band is double-clicked ss loops that cannot take the full complement
hypotheses.mechanism: The ~26 kDa species in lane 2 is a mix of open single-click conjugates (dangling BCN) and double-click ss loops. These have the same mass, and the loop is more compact, so the two co-migrate inside the broad, saturated 26 kDa band. Lane 3 resolves 26 kDa into a 421/425 px doublet. The ~35 kDa lane-2 band is most simply sfGFP with two separate ssDNAs (one per Tet, apparent shift +8 kDa per ssDNA, additive). With cDNA: (a) open conjugates hybridise freely and become sfGFP-dsDNA rods at ~30 kDa; (b) sfGFP(ssDNA)2 gains two duplexes and moves into the 43-60 kDa region, which rises from ~13% to ~18%; (c) closed loops resist hybridisation. Full zipping of a linear complement onto a 50-nt circle closed by the protein needs the complement's free tail to thread through the shrinking loop about 4.8 times. It also needs ~23 kT of bending (A/2·L/R², L = 170 Å, R = 43 Å), plus twist and end-orientation mismatch at the fixed Tet sites. Any partial hybrid either never forms or is stripped in SDS. On this view the 1-Tet 'no shift' result is not comparable: it was on a different gel, the open 1-Tet adduct may run elsewhere, or 1-Tet + bis-BCN went mostly to sfGFP-DNA-sfGFP dumbbells.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Explains the ~50:50 split of single-DNA conjugates between the shifted (~30) and unshifted (~26) bands without invoking limiting cDNA. cDNA is 10 µM against ≤10 µM total ssDNA, so it is in effective excess, and the free-DNA duplex takes only ~20-30%. A non-hybridising population must exist, and the strained loop is the obvious one. It also explains the loss of the ~35 kDa band and the rise of the high-MW region. The sharp, smear-free ~30 band (no density at 409-417 px) fits a stable, unstrained duplex. It does not explain the 1-Tet result as reported, so it requires that control to be flawed.
hypotheses.explains_em: Well. Dot at the end of a straight rod (26% of the rod stream) is the open sfGFP-dsDNA 'lollipop'. Single dots (18% of the anchor stream) include loops whose ssDNA is invisible. Free rods (143 Å, the same as the free-DNA control) are unconjugated duplex. No rings, because no closed duplex exists. 'Two dots + faint thread' (70-100 Å apart) are sfGFP-ssDNA-sfGFP from the high-MW gel bands.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: Rods attached to dots should be full-length 50 bp. Their projected length distribution should match the free-rod and free-DNA-control distribution (~143 Å, same foreshortening statistics) once the 200 Å 2D window truncation is removed. The adversarial review shows the dot-class far ends sit 64-99 Å from the box centre, so the current '~100 Å DNA' may be mask-limited. Test: re-extract dot-at-end particles in a 400 Å box and run 2D with a 320 Å window, or trace rods directly on denoised micrographs. The 87 Å 'dot + short rod' class should then be explained by tilt foreshortening alone, i.e. it should be in the same proportion as short projections in the free-rod population. Dot-rod contacts above the crowding null should be ~25-30% of sfGFP dots.
hypotheses.bench_test: A Tet-capture chase using reagents already in the condition table. After the click (before cDNA), add excess TCO-PEG5k. Open 2-Tet mono-adducts still carry a free Tet and gain +5 kDa PEG (large SDS shift). Closed loops have no free Tet and do not shift. In parallel, add excess methyltetrazine-PEG2k, which reacts with the dangling BCN of open adducts only. Then add cDNA and ask which population makes the ~30 kDa band. Run 1-Tet and 2-Tet, each ±cDNA, on the same gel, and heat-melt a lane-3 aliquot (75 °C, 2 min) to confirm that ~30 reverts to ~26.

hypotheses.name: H3: The ~30 kDa band is the closed loop holding a partially hybridised, topologically trapped complement (a yielded spring), not a full 50 bp ring
hypotheses.mechanism: The double-click loop forms. cDNA nucleates and zips only until threading or strain stops it. With the cDNA tail unable to thread through the protein-closed loop, the remaining ss segment can absorb only ~1-2 turns of compensating writhe. That leaves ~10-25 bp of duplex plus ~25-40 nt of ss loop, with the rest of the cDNA as a dangling ss tail; the alternative is a kinked or melted bubble, as in Zocchi's yielding. The complex carries the whole complement mass, so on SDS-PAGE it shifts like a hybrid and stays bound (10-25 bp at 10 µM, unboiled). The topology (closed loop plus wound strand) may add retardation. Open mono-adducts hybridise fully but co-migrate with the ss open adduct, or sit at ~35 kDa and move up. Either way this fits the user's 1-Tet result.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Fits the band pattern and the 1-Tet observation: only 2-Tet loops give the new ~30 band. The ~half of loops left at ~26 kDa are loops where nucleation failed or the partial hybrid was stripped. It also fits the sharp ~30 band: the trapped complex is kinetically stable.
hypotheses.explains_em: Best of the hypotheses. ssDNA (the rest of the loop and the cDNA tail) is essentially invisible in 200 kV cryo-EM of crowded ice. Each complex therefore looks like an sfGFP dot carrying a SHORT straight duplex stub (10-25 bp = 35-85 Å), with no hole. This matches the 'dot + short rod' anchor class (87 Å total, DNA ~57 Å ≈ 17 bp) and part of 'dot + long rod'. Free rods are the full 50 bp duplex from unconjugated ssDNA + cDNA. The one-ended bright blob 18-31 Å inside the rod_no_dot ends is consistent with a dot overlapping a short stub. No closed loops in 304 classes, as observed.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: Projected lengths of dot-attached duplex should be shorter than free rods even with an enlarged window: a distinct mode at ~35-85 Å (about 1-2 helical turns), not a foreshortening tail of the 143 Å distribution. The free-rod population should be ~20-30% of the DNA count and full-length. Stubs should leave the dot near-tangentially (from the Tet-133/149 face), with a consistent angle to the barrel long axis in dot-centred 2D. A faint ss arc may appear in high-particle-count averages after tight alignment on the dot.
hypotheses.bench_test: Use a Cy5-labelled cDNA and image both channels. The ~30 kDa band should carry one cDNA per sfGFP. Mung bean or S1 nuclease, which cuts ss only, should cleave the ~30 species and shorten its DNA. Place a restriction site at 3-4 positions along the 50 bp and digest the purified ~30 species (or protect with DNase I): only sites inside the paired stub are cut. Decisive variant: use a complement split into two 25-mers, or hybridise before the second click, either of which needs no threading. If the threading barrier is the cause, full springs and a band distinct from ~30 kDa should appear.

hypotheses.name: H4: Few loops form; the ~26 kDa band is mostly open mono-adducts, the ~30 kDa band is their hybrids, and incomplete hybridisation leaves the rest
hypotheses.mechanism: The second Tet is often unusable or slow to close. Tetrazine ncAAs are partly reduced to the dihydro form in E. coli; site 149 or 133 may have poor BCN access; the TEG-BCN geometry may disfavour the 31 Å closure. A kinetic check from lane 2: if the ~35 kDa band (~10%) is sfGFP(ssDNA)2, its ratio to the ~26 kDa band (≥49%) means intermolecular capture by ~10 µM free BCN competed with closure at ~1:5. That puts the effective closure molarity near 50 µM, an order of magnitude below the ~0.3-1 mM expected for a flexible 50-nt loop. So many ~26 kDa species are probably open. cDNA then hybridises only ~half of the open adducts, because it is sub-stoichiometric (oligo quantitation, cDNA secondary structure, competition from free ssDNA) or because some of the duplex is lost in the SDS loading buffer.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Explains the ~30 band as the plain hybridised conjugate (+4 kDa apparent on top of the +8 for ssDNA). It also explains the large loss of the ~35 band into the high-MW region. It needs the 1-Tet 'no shift' to be an artefact of that control (different gel, low 1-Tet conjugation, mostly dumbbells). It struggles with the absence of a smear, which argues against in-gel dissociation, so the unshifted half must be unhybridised before loading.
hypotheses.explains_em: Dot at the end of a full-length straight rod as the main conjugate; single dots as unhybridised conjugates (ss invisible); no loops because almost none formed.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: Same rod-length prediction as H2 (attached rods full length after window correction), but a higher ratio of dot-rod to single-dot conjugates. The gel predicts ~0.3 hybridised conjugates per sfGFP in lane 3, i.e. ~100 dot-rod contacts above the crowding null per micrograph. Under H2, unhybridised loops add single dots; under H4 the single dots are ss open adducts and should sometimes show a faint 'thread' tail.
hypotheses.bench_test: Intact-protein LC-MS of the click mixture after a small-molecule TCO quench. Each unreacted Tet gains the quencher mass, so you can count 0/1/2 consumed Tets: the loop has 2 consumed, the open adduct 1 plus quench. Check cDNA stoichiometry with a cDNA titration (0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4×). If the ~30:~26 ratio keeps rising with cDNA, the cause is incomplete hybridisation, not strain.

hypotheses.name: H5: The ~30 kDa signal is partly a gel or loading artefact, or an sfGFP conformer, and over-reports any DNA product
hypotheses.mechanism: Lane 1 (sfGFP only) already has faint bands at the ~30 and ~28 kDa positions (~8% each of lane fluorescence), at exactly the same pixel row (403 px) as the new lane-3 band. These are probably a partly unfolded fluorescent conformer or a disulfide or folding dimer (C48/C70). Lane-to-lane variation is large: free sfGFP should not depend on cDNA, yet it moves from ~19% to ~11% between lanes 2 and 3. Fluorescence is not a molar readout. Site 149 sits next to His148, which contacts the chromophore, and a strained or conjugated sfGFP can be dimmer or more SDS-labile. The image is an 8-bit composite with saturated bands (lane-2 26 kDa band and lane-1 free band at 254). Part of the 'shift' may therefore be a cDNA-promoted, DNA-mediated change in conformer or brightness rather than a defined new species.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Explains the coincident 403 px position and the shaky densitometry (the stated lane-1 baselines of 20% and 12% mostly integrate background). It cannot explain the full ~28-point cDNA-dependent rise on its own, so at most it is a modifier of H1-H4.
hypotheses.explains_em: Neutral: EM then reflects H2-H4 chemistry with a smaller true conjugate fraction.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: The EM fraction of dots with a rod above the crowding null should be well below the ~25-30% that the gel implies.
hypotheses.bench_test: Re-run on one gel with a non-saturating exposure: sfGFP ± cDNA alone, sfGFP + free (non-BCN) ssDNA + cDNA, 1-Tet and 2-Tet ± cDNA. Use the same samples boiled and stained with Coomassie or anti-His so that species are counted by molecule, not by fluorescence.

key_references: Gel re-analysis of /n/home05/ianpoon/DNA-springs-project-2026-27/cryoEM/image.png (my local-background lane profiles, 8-bit, saturated in the lane-2 26 kDa and lane-1 free bands). Rows: 35k = 390 px, 30k = 403 px, 26k = 421-426 px (lane 3 shows a 421/425 px doublet), free sfGFP = 474/479 px doublet. Fractions of lane fluorescence, high-MW region included. Lane 1: free 74%, 30k 8%, 28k 7%, 26k 4%, >40k 4%. Lane 2: free 19%, 26k ≥49% (saturated), 35k 10%, >40k 13%, ~10 kDa 5%, 30k <3%. Lane 3: free 11%, 30k 31%, 26k 33%, 35k 3%, >40k 18%. Implied: ~45-50% of single-DNA conjugates convert to the ~30 kDa species; the ~35 kDa (probably sfGFP(ssDNA)2) band moves into the >40k region; and a ~8-point drift in free sfGFP between lanes 2 and 3 sets the noise floor. The stated lane-1 'baselines' (20%/12%) mostly integrate background, except a real faint sfGFP-only band at the 403 px row.

On the 1-Tet control: it shows only that the cDNA-dependent band needs the second Tet. Species that need the second Tet include the ss loop, a partially hybridised loop, a fully hybridised loop, and sfGFP(ssDNA)2. It cannot tell a full spring from a partially or topologically trapped hybrid on a loop (H1 vs H3), and that is the distinction that matters for EM. For it to rule out open hybrids, four things must hold on the SAME gel: (i) 1-Tet + bis-BCN ssDNA gives a mono-adduct band of comparable intensity; (ii) where that band runs, ~26 or ~35 kDa, also assigns the 2-Tet bands; (iii) cDNA demonstrably hybridises to it (native PAGE/SYBR or Cy5-cDNA); (iv) the result is not dominated by sfGFP-DNA-sfGFP dumbbells. If 'no shift' is real, SDS-PAGE is blind to hybridisation of open conjugates, and the ~30 kDa retardation must then come from topology, i.e. a closed ring of protein + DNA. That is itself a strong, testable claim.

Bending-energy estimate for the full 50 bp ring: E ≈ (A/2)·L/R² with A = 50 nm·kT, L = 17 nm, R = 4.3 nm, giving ~23 kT (~14 kcal/mol), before twist and end-orientation mismatch. This is below the ~−60 to −70 kcal/mol of 50-mer hybridisation, so the barrier is more likely kinetic or topological (threading of the cDNA tail through the protein-closed loop) than thermodynamic.

Expected EM abundance under H1: lane-3 ~30 kDa band ≈ 25-30% of folded sfGFP, about 80-100 rings per micrograph at ~330 sfGFP per 291 nm micrograph. Zero hole-bearing classes in 304 argues strongly against intact rings at the abundance the gel implies.

Window caveat from /n/home05/ianpoon/DNA-springs-project-2026-27/cryoEM/sfgfp_chimera_screening/results/rod_end_coloc_review.json: the 200 Å 2D inner window truncates dot-centred rods (far ends 64-99 Å from the box centre). So '~100 Å DNA' on dot + long rod may be mask-limited. The 87 Å dot + short rod class is not, and it is the most direct existing-data discriminator between H2/H4 (full-length attached rods) and H3 (short stubs).

Zocchi G and co-workers: DNA 'molecular springs' on proteins and the yielding/kinking of strongly bent duplexes (Choi B, Zocchi G, JACS 2006; Qu H, Tseng CY, Wang Y, Levine AJ, Zocchi G, EPL 2010; Qu H, Zocchi G, EPL 2011). These cover the yielding model the MD contradicts.

Cloutier TE, Widom J, Mol Cell 2004; Du Q, Smith C, Shiffeldrim N, Vologodskaia M, Vologodskii A, PNAS 2005; Vafabakhsh R, Ha T, Science 2012. These are on the J-factor and bendability of <100 bp loops.
Kool ET, Annu Rev Biophys Biomol Struct 1996: circular oligonucleotides, binding of linear strands to small ss circles, and the topological limits on full pairing.
Pédelacq JD et al., Nat Biotechnol 2006 (superfolder GFP). The semi-native, unboiled SDS-PAGE behaviour of GFP is anomalously fast and in-gel fluorescent.

Blizzard RJ et al., JACS 2015 (Tet-v2.0 genetic encoding, tetrazine-strained alkene kinetics); Jang HS et al., ACS Cent Sci 2020 (Tet3.0, including in-cell tetrazine reduction to the dihydro form, which can leave one Tet site dead).
Trads JB, Tørring T, Gothelf KV, Acc Chem Res 2017: protein-DNA conjugates. Conjugate SDS-PAGE mobility is anomalous: each ssDNA here adds ~8 kDa apparent for ~16 kDa real.

hypotheses.name: H1. Few or no closed loops formed. The ~30 kDa band is linear sfGFP-dsDNA (or another product specific to 2-Tet), and the dot-at-rod-end classes are linear adducts or chance contacts
hypotheses.mechanism: The second intramolecular click fails, so loops never close. Three possible causes, any one enough: (a) cDNA was in the tube during the click. The 'reacted 1:1:1 at 10 uM each' wording suggests it was. Hybridisation at 10 uM takes seconds to minutes, while BCN-tetrazine clicks at 10 uM take hours. Once the strand is a 50 bp duplex (~170 A long), its free BCN end must bend ~222 deg to reach a Tet 31 A away. That costs ~22 kT for a smooth arc (P=500 A), so the closure J-factor is <<1 nM, far below the 10 uM available for intermolecular reaction. The outcome is linear mono-adducts, bridged dumbbells and short chains. (b) One of the two Tet sites in a fraction of the protein is unreactive. On-protein Tet reduction and near-cognate UAG read-through have been reported for Tet ncAAs (Eddins/Mehl 2023), so part of the '2-Tet' protein is effectively 1-Tet. (c) BCN-Tet kinetics leave the reaction incomplete. In this reading, adding cDNA shifts only the conjugates whose DNA is accessible. The '1-Tet gives no shift' result would then come from a non-equivalent control, for example lower 1-Tet conjugation yield, a different gel or run, or a bridged (1-Tet)2-ssDNA band hiding the shift.
hypotheses.explains_gel: Lane 3's new ~30 kDa band is cDNA hybridised onto ssDNA that is attached to sfGFP at one end. It can only form when cDNA is present, as observed. Two weaknesses. First, ~32 percentage points of the 26 kDa species stay unshifted in lane 3 even though cDNA is stoichiometric, so H1 needs a cDNA shortfall, competition from free ssDNA, or an ss species that cannot hybridise. Second, it must explain away the 1-Tet control. Densitometry caveat: lane 1 (sfGFP only) already has ~20% of its signal at ~30 kDa and 12% at ~26 kDa, so the band that depends on cDNA is ~20-28 points net, not 40%. The faint ladder of bands above 34 kDa in lanes 2 and 3 fits intermolecular bridging.
hypotheses.explains_em: Fits the EM directly, with no special pleading. Expected class mapping: dot at the end of a straight rod (26%) = linear sfGFP-dsDNA adduct, plus chance contacts in a crowded field (~0.06 dots per rod end by chance at 3,900 dots/um2), plus picking and 2D bias. Free rods (19%) = unconjugated 2-BCN duplex, which the fluorescence gel cannot see; their one-ended blob may be BCN-TEG or an end effect, and the free-DNA control shows the same protrusion. Single dots and anchor dot pairs = free sfGFP and sfGFP-ssDNA; 50 nt of ssDNA is invisible at 200 kV. Two dots + faint thread (16%) = sfGFP-ssDNA-sfGFP bridges or chance pairs. No rings, because there are no loops. The DNA length of ~100 A in dot+rod classes, against 143 A for free rods, is mostly an artefact: those classes are centred on the dot, and the 200 A 2D window cuts off density about 85 A past the dot edge.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) Re-extract the dot+long-rod particles centred on the rod midpoint (box >=400 A) and redo 2D with a window >=320 A. The DNA length should then match free rods run through the same pipeline (~140-150 A), and the 34 A helical repeat should be visible. (2) Projected mass per unit length, integrated across the rod profile, should equal that of free rods within ~10%, with no tapering towards the dot. (3) The dot should sit at a broad range of angles to the rod axis, because the TEG linker acts as a hinge. (4) Dot-pair spacing g(r) should show an excess near ~190-220 A with a rod between the pair (dsDNA dumbbells), on top of the crowding baseline. (5) The ratio of attached to free rods per micrograph should roughly match the gel conjugation fraction.
hypotheses.bench_test: Run one gel with all the controls side by side: 2-Tet sfGFP + mono-BCN ssDNA + cDNA (a linear reference on the same protein), 1-Tet + 2-BCN ssDNA with and without cDNA, and 2-Tet with and without cDNA. Add order-of-addition arms: click 24 h then add cDNA, against all three premixed. Chase the crude mix with the TCO-PEG5k already in the reagent table; a free Tet then gains a large mobility shift, while closed loops have no free Tet. Also chase with a methyltetrazine-dye, which labels any dangling BCN. Post-stain with SYBR Gold, or use Cy5-cDNA, to show which bands carry cDNA. Check that each Tet reacts by PEGylating 2-Tet sfGFP alone and confirming that two PEG adducts form.

hypotheses.name: H2. Loops formed in solution but did not survive at the air-water interface. Strained duplexes peel or melt, or sfGFP unfolds, and the products are bare dots and invisible ssDNA
hypotheses.mechanism: The particle density shows that essentially every particle sits on an air-water interface (AWI). At 10 uM, ~30 nm of ice should hold ~180 particles/um2 on average, but the data show ~3,900/um2, a ~20x surface enrichment, consistent with Noble 2018 (~90% at the AWI). Proteins partly denature at the AWI (D'Imprima 2019). A closed duplex arc storing ~22 kT and pushing at 25-36 pN (the MD result) is the species most prone to strain-assisted unstacking and peeling at a hydrophobic interface during blotting and in the thin film. sfGFP may also unravel locally between residues 133 and 149 under a sustained 30 pN load. The ring could then open into a sfGFP carrying a ss or partly ss loop, with the cDNA released or left as short duplex segments.
hypotheses.explains_gel: The gel shows the solution state, so the user's reading stands: the ~30 kDa band is the hybridised loop (if the 1-Tet control is equivalent, linear hybrids do not shift).
hypotheses.explains_em: Rings are absent because they are destroyed or melted before vitrification. sfGFP carrying a ss loop appears as single dots or a dot with faint fuzz; a partly re-annealed loop appears as a dot plus a short rod (the 12% at 87 A). Unstrained species, such as free duplex and linear adducts, survive, which is why free rods are abundant and show B-DNA repeats. The high 'ice' and 'junk' fractions (32%) fit a harsh AWI.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) Fewer rods than input: duplex rods per micrograph should fall well short of the ~1:1 DNA:sfGFP input after allowing for picker recall, and the shortfall should scale with the gel loop fraction. (2) Single-dot class averages should show an extra diffuse halo or tail compared with clean sfGFP views. (3) Split micrographs by CTF-estimated ice thickness: any ring-like or curved-rod classes, and the dot+rod fraction, should be enriched in the thickest-ice tertile. (4) Smeared or enlarged dot classes would indicate partial sfGFP unfolding.
hypotheses.bench_test: Change how the grids are made while keeping the sample the same. Compare a graphene-oxide or thin-carbon support (which adsorbs particles away from the AWI) with an open-hole grid. Also try a surfactant compatible with DNA (for example 0.05% CHAPSO or fluorinated octyl maltoside) and a 10x dilution, which also fixes the crowding. In parallel, image the same crude mix by negative stain on carbon or by liquid AFM on Ni2+-mica. If rings appear on a support or by AFM but not on open-hole cryo grids, H2 is supported. In solution, the strained loop should show a lower duplex melting temperature than the linear control (SYBR melt).

hypotheses.name: H3. Loops exist on the grid but are yielded or collapsed: one kink or melted bubble, or a partial duplex closed by ss, so the projection is a dot plus a short thick rod with no resolvable hole
hypotheses.mechanism: The unyielded arc (~22 kT) can relax in three ways. (i) A central melted bubble or kink acts as a hinge, and the two ~23-25 bp arms fold into a narrow V. With arms ~78 A and a base of ~45-60 A (31 A between Tet sites plus the TEG linkers), the apex angle is ~35-45 deg and the open hole is ~15 A across, below 12 A 2D resolution once sfGFP covers the base. (ii) Only ~30-35 bp anneal into a straight segment of ~100-115 A, and the remaining 15-20 nt of ss closes back to sfGFP; the ss part is invisible. (iii) Lying flat on the AWI pushes the loop further into a hairpin. This is the Zocchi-type yielding the MD has not yet shown, possibly driven by the AWI. In every case the molecule is still topologically a loop.
hypotheses.explains_gel: The user's reading stands: the ~30 kDa band is the cDNA-hybridised loop; a kinked or partial duplex still adds the cDNA mass. The loop-specific shift (absent with 1-Tet) is credible if a compact or topologically linked hybrid runs differently in the gel or holds onto its cDNA more tightly than a linear hybrid.
hypotheses.explains_em: The yielded loops are the dot + rod classes. Dot + long rod has ~100 A of DNA, which matches the partial-duplex arm (ii) or a V seen slightly side-on. Dot + short rod (87 A total, ~57 A of DNA) matches a V arm length or a tilted view. No ring classes appear because no hole can be resolved. Edge-on views of an intact ring would also look like a ~90-110 A bar with a dot (label guide, 'closed loop edge-on'). That is why the absence of rings, though strong evidence against open circular rings, says little against collapsed loops.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: This is the most direct test available in the data now. (1) After re-centring with a large window, as in H1, the attached DNA length stays <=100-115 A, against ~145 A for free rods in the same pipeline. Here H1 and H3 make opposite predictions. (2) Projected mass per unit length of attached rods is ~1.5-2x that of free rods near the dot (V model) or ~1x with an invisible ss return (model ii). The rod is wider at the dot end (>=40 A) and tapers towards the tip. (3) The 34 A helical repeat is lost: superposed arms are out of register, or the segment is kinked. (4) The rod leaves the dot near the dot's centre at a narrower range of angles than with a linear TEG hinge. (5) A focused sub-classification of the dot+rod subset (~100 classes, mask covering rod and dot) may split the V into two arms or show a faint return thread.
hypotheses.bench_test: Treat the crude lane-3 mix and a linear-adduct control with S1/P1 nuclease or KMnO4. A bubble or kink in a strained loop is cut or modified, and because both arms stay attached, the loop band changes topology without losing mass, while the linear duplex control is resistant. Map where the kink sits by sequencing the cut sites. Gel-purify or SEC-purify the ~30 kDa species, image it alone (negative stain, then cryo at ~1 uM on graphene oxide), and repeat with cDNAs that leave a deliberate 10-15 nt gap (an ss hinge, as a positive control for the V shape) or that are fully complementary.

hypotheses.name: H4. ss loops close, but cDNA cannot fully anneal to them (strain or topology). cDNA shifts only open mono-adducts, and the loops look like bare dots
hypotheses.mechanism: With ssDNA (P ~20 A, contour ~315 A) the effective molarity for the second click is ~0.4 mM, ~40x the 10 uM intermolecular concentration, so bis-clicked ss loops form readily when the click runs first. A linear cDNA annealing to a strand closed through the protein has to wind about 4.8 times around it, and its free tail has to thread through a hole that shrinks as the duplex grows. Each added base pair also adds bending strain, up to ~22 kT. Annealing is still favoured thermodynamically overall (~-100 kT), but it may stall kinetically at a few short paranemic or partial segments that the SDS gel strips off. Mono-adducts with a free BCN end hybridise normally.
hypotheses.explains_gel: The unshifted 26 kDa band left in lane 3 (44%, net ~32 points) is the ss loop, which cannot take cDNA, and the ~30 kDa band is the linear mono-adduct hybrid. This explains the unshifted fraction despite stoichiometric cDNA better than H1 does. It conflicts with the reported 1-Tet result: a 1-Tet mono-adduct should shift as well, so that control would have to be non-equivalent.
hypotheses.explains_em: Loops carry only ssDNA, which is invisible, so they appear as single dots (18% of the anchor stream) or chance dot pairs. They can never form ring classes. Dot + rod classes are the linear hybrids. Free rods are free duplex.
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) The number of dot+rod particles per micrograph should match the net ~30 kDa fraction (~20-28% of sfGFP, ~65-90 per micrograph before picker recall), while bare dots dominate. (2) Attached rods behave as in H1: full ~145 A length once re-centred, 1x mass per length, 34 A repeat. (3) Bare-dot class averages show a faint ss halo compared with clean sfGFP. (4) No dumbbells, because the loop has no free BCN.
hypotheses.bench_test: Chase with TCO-PEG5k plus a methyltetrazine-dye. The unshifted 26 kDa species gains neither label if it is an ss loop (no free Tet and no free BCN); a linear mono-adduct gains both. S1 nuclease removes the ss from the 26 kDa species. Raising the temperature during annealing (a slow ramp from 65 C, which sfGFP tolerates briefly) should convert stalled loops into the ~30 kDa band if the block is kinetic.

hypotheses.name: H5. Intact open rings are present and abundant, but picking, 2D design, crowding or heterogeneity hid them
hypotheses.mechanism: Rings may have been missed because neither picking stream centres on them. The rod picker fires on straight segments; the dot picker centres on sfGFP, which puts the far side of the ring ~110 A from the box centre, at the edge of the 200 A window. Rings in a crowded field (NN spacing ~80 A, ~1.2 extra dots per 200 A window) may also have been scattered across dot-pair or junk classes. Heterogeneous loop shapes and tilts may have blurred any average.
hypotheses.explains_gel: The user's reading stands: the ~30 kDa band is the hybridised loop, ~20-28% of sfGFP.
hypotheses.explains_em: This is weak. If 20-28% of sfGFP were rings, the dataset would hold ~66-92 per micrograph, ~0.5-0.7 M in total. Even 1% recovery would give a ring class at 12 A. A 66 A hole is ~5x the resolution limit. Crowding puts only ~0.13 chance dots inside an average hole. The label guide shows that simulated loops in this real ice are obvious, and DNA has high contrast here (free rods show a 34 A repeat). An anchor-centred ring would still appear as a dot plus a curved hook. No curved rods or hooks appear in the sheets. So the absence of rings is strong evidence that rings with an open hole, face-on or tilted up to ~50 deg, are absent from the vitrified sample (well under ~1-2% of sfGFP). It is weak evidence about the solution state (H2) and says nothing against collapsed or edge-on loops (H3).
hypotheses.predicts_in_existing_em_data: (1) Template-pick the existing real micrographs with projections of the L6_loop50 model at several tilts, and in parallel with a matched straight-rod decoy template. Run 2D with a 260-300 A window. Under H5, ring classes appear that are absent from the decoy picks. (2) Re-run 2D on the anchor stream with a larger window (>=300 A), or re-centre on the dot plus 60 A, and look for arcs or hooks. (3) Score the curvature of every rod-stream particle; H5 predicts a population of curvature radii ~40-50 A.
hypotheses.bench_test: Negative stain or cryo-EM at 0.5-1 uM on graphene oxide of the gel- or SEC-purified ~30 kDa species. Without crowding and free DNA, rings should be obvious by eye if they exist.
